questions.q: What is a Salesforce Certified Technical Architect (CTA) review board actually testing, per this lesson?
options: Whether the judges personally like the proposed design
How quickly the candidate can type out a presentation document
Whether the candidate actually understands the tradeoffs behind their own decisions well enough to defend them under pressure, or credibly revise them when a judge surfaces a real gap
Whether the candidate has memorized every Salesforce governor limit
questions.explain: The judges are trained not to signal approval or disapproval -- the test is specifically about defending or appropriately revising the reasoning under challenge, not whether the design is liked.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say designing a good tradeoff analysis and defending it live under challenge are genuinely different skills?
options: Because defending a design requires no preparation at all
Because Salesforce review boards do not allow any Q&A period
Because designs presented live are always technically different from designs presented in writing
Because the second skill -- defending a decision when someone pushes back with a scenario you didn't originally consider -- only gets built through practice, not by reading about it
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly separates these as two skills, and frames this lesson's practice format as the way to build the defense skill specifically, since reading about challenge rounds doesn't substitute for practicing them.

questions.q: What does this lesson recommend as the stronger response when a challenge surfaces a genuine gap in a design?
options: Acknowledging the gap and revising the position, since demonstrating that update is exactly the skill being tested, rather than defending something that's actually wrong
Defending the original position regardless of the gap, to appear confident
Ending the presentation immediately
Changing the subject to a different part of the design
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly states that saying 'that's a fair point, I'd need to revisit this because X' demonstrates the skill being tested, and that defending an indefensible position after a judge has found the hole is the worse outcome.

questions.q: What habit does this lesson recommend for pointing a challenger to why a specific decision was made, rather than repeating general tradeoff reasoning?
options: Quoting a Trailhead module title as justification
Citing the specific scenario fact that actually drove the decision, such as 'this is a nightly financial reconciliation with no same-day requirement,' rather than a generic rule of thumb
Refusing to answer any question about why the alternative wasn't chosen
Repeating the decision louder without adding any new information
questions.explain: Grounding the answer in the scenario's actual stated facts shows the decision wasn't a reflex -- it survives a challenge better than a generic restatement of the general tradeoff reasoning.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why does an ADR written per Lesson 8's format make the 'why not the other side' challenge question easier to answer during a review board?
options: Because ADRs are not relevant to review board preparation
Because ADRs eliminate the need for any Q&A period
Because the ADR's rationale section already names what was traded away, which is close to guaranteed to be exactly what a challenger asks about
Because review boards only accept answers that quote an ADR verbatim
questions.explain: Since Lesson 8's rationale section specifically names the cost that was traded away, a candidate who already wrote one has most of the 'why not the other side' answer prepared before the question is even asked.
